lede: A Malaysian probability party game. Everyone can see what is in the jar; nobody knows the order it comes out in. Read the odds, bet on secret predictions, and play friends in rooms that need no server.

body: Balang is built around one shared jar of familiar Malaysian kuih. Players know exactly what goes in. As tokens are drawn, they keep reassessing the odds, drop predictions that are becoming unlikely, lock their final choices, and decide whether to risk KAW-KAW.
The goal was a game that is easy to understand in the first round, strategic without needing advanced maths, and fast enough that people want another match straight away.

items.title: Read the jar
items.detail: 25 tokens of five kuih, chosen at random from a pool of ten each round. The counts are public; the order is secret.

items.title: Predict
items.detail: Each player gets six secret prediction cards, such as “more onde-onde than dodol” or “muruku exactly 3”. Harder predictions are worth more.

items.title: Draw
items.detail: Players take turns to shake the jar. 14 tokens come out and 11 stay in.

items.title: Discard and lock
items.detail: After draw 5 you drop two cards and after draw 9 one more. After draw 12 all three remaining cards count: you place one on the negative side, where it costs you its value if it comes true.

items.title: KAW-KAW
items.detail: You may go KAW-KAW on one positive card: double its value if it comes true, lose its value if it does not.

items.title: Win
items.detail: Positive cards that come true score their value; a negative card that comes true loses it. Three rounds; the highest total is JUARA.

value.label: Balang multiplayer architecture
value.caption: The host’s browser holds every secret; each guest only ever receives its own filtered view.

nodes.title: Host creates room
nodes.detail: Buat Bilik: the host browser becomes the game authority.

nodes.title: Game engine
nodes.detail: Pure TypeScript state machine: draw order, hands, scoring, bots.

nodes.title: Pricing
nodes.detail: Card rewards priced from probability at deal time (Monte Carlo).

nodes.title: WebRTC
nodes.detail: Guests join by code, link or QR over PeerJS.

nodes.title: Filtered views
nodes.detail: Each guest sees only their own cards and the public jar.

sections.headline: Built to be fair and to survive dropouts.

items.title: Engine separate from UI
items.detail: src/engine holds the game logic, prediction types, probability pricing, bots and statistics; the React UI only renders state.

items.title: 12 prediction types
items.detail: Each card type has its own evaluation and an “already decided” check, so cards can be stamped DAH PASTI or DAH GAGAL as soon as the outcome is certain.

items.title: Probability-priced rewards
items.detail: Rewards come from the card’s chance of success at deal time, estimated with Monte Carlo simulation, and all balancing values live in one config file.

items.title: Bots
items.detail: Bots play empty seats, and take over a guest’s turns if they disconnect until they rejoin from the same browser.

items.title: Turn timer
items.detail: If the host sets a time limit and it runs out, a token is drawn or a card chosen automatically.

items.title: Assets pipeline
items.detail: Sprites are sliced from the concept sheets by a Python script, so the art can be regenerated.

body: A reward table that looks fair on paper can still be broken in play. Because the engine runs without the UI, bots can play whole matches on their own and report how the rewards behave. The first report showed the game was too forgiving: about three in four locked cards came true, so the final choice carried little risk. That led to the final rules, borrowed from the board game Bag of Chips: every final card counts and one must go on the negative side. In the same bot matches, that negative card now costs its owner points in about a third of rounds.

items.title: Put the rules in one place
items.detail: A pure engine with tests made every UI change safe and makes balance testing possible.

items.title: Trust boundaries matter even in games
items.detail: Keeping secrets on the host and sending filtered views stopped the easiest way to cheat.

items.title: Numbers should feel honest
items.detail: Each card is priced from its real chance of coming true, so a risky prediction pays more because it is genuinely less likely.
